Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, what brings me in... well, it's—it's my talking, mostly. Or my thinking? I don't even know anymore, to be honest. I work as an orderly, you know, a psych aide over at the hospital, mostly doing the overnight shifts because the pay is a little better and I only have my high school diploma, so I have to take what I can get, right? 

But lately, I just... I can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore. It's like they're just spilling out all wrong. Like, the other morning, I was trying to give a quick rundown to the day-shift nurse about how my overnight shift went, just basic stuff about who slept and who didn't. But then suddenly I start talking about soccer, because I used to play back in school and someone had a ball on the TV, and then from there I'm talking about the paint colors on the walls in the dayroom, and then I'm jumping right back to the patient charts—but not even the right charts, just the concept of the folders themselves. 

And I can just see it in their faces. I can see everyone getting completely lost. The nurses look at me like I'm speaking a different language, and I'm standing there knowing I started at point A but somehow ended up at point Z, and I can't even retrace my steps to figure out how I got there. It's just happening all the time now. Every time I try to explain something simple, it turns into this huge tangled mess that doesn't connect, and it's making it really, really hard to do my job or even just have a normal conversation without people staring at me.

Yeah, sad. Definitely sad. I mean, not just sad like, "Oh, I had a bad day at work," but this deep, heavy kind of sad that just... it doesn't go away. It's like I wake up in the afternoon, because of the night shift, right? And before I even get out of bed, before my feet even hit the floor, I just feel this massive weight on my chest. It's just so heavy, and empty at the same time, if that even makes sense. Like there's nothing inside me but lead. 

And it's most days now. It really is. I'll drag myself out of bed, make that terrible coffee I told you about, put on my scrubs, and just sort of... go through the motions. And then, when the shift is over, around 7 AM when everyone else is, you know, going to get their morning drinks or heading home to sleep... I get out to the parking lot, and the sun is coming up, and it's supposed to be a new day, but I just get into my car and I can't even put the key in the ignition. I just sit there behind the wheel, staring at the dashboard, and I just start crying. For no reason. I mean, nobody yelled at me, none of the patients threw anything at me that night, it was a totally normal shift, but I'll just sit in the driver's seat and cry for like twenty, thirty minutes before I can even pull myself together enough to drive the ten minutes back to my apartment. 

It's just this overwhelming sadness that I can't shake. I try to tell myself, you know, "You have a job, you're paying rent, you're doing fine," but my brain just doesn't care. It just feels like everything is pointless and exhausting. So yeah, definitely sad. Not really anxious or irritable, just... really, really sad and empty. All the time.

Well, the thing with my words getting all mixed up, that's been going on for a while now. It's not just a recent thing, you know? It's been... gosh, I'd say about a year and a month. Yeah, thirteen months. I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time I first got this feeling that I was being watched. 

See, about a year and a month ago, I started noticing things at work. Little things at first. Like, I'd be walking down the C-wing, and I'd get this intense, prickling sensation on the back of my neck, like someone's eyes were just boring into me. I thought maybe it was one of the patients, you know, staring out from their room, but I'd turn around and the hallway would be completely empty. And then it started happening in the breakroom, too. I'd be sitting there, trying to eat my lukewarm microwave dinner at 2 AM, and I'd just know, with absolute certainty, that someone—or something—was observing me. Monitoring me. 

And it wasn't just at the hospital, either. I'd go home to my apartment, lock the door, pull the blinds down tight, and I still couldn't shake the feeling. I'd sit on my couch in the dark, just waiting, listening to the pipes creak, completely convinced that there were cameras hidden in the vents or that the neighbors were tracking my movements through the floorboards. It sounds crazy when I say it out loud, I know it does, but it felt so real. It still feels real sometimes. 

And right around that same time, that's when the talking thing started. The disorganized stuff. Like I'd be trying to tell the charge nurse that room 412 needed fresh linens, and instead I'd start talking about how the laundry carts were aligned with the magnetic poles or something, and my sentences would just unravel. I'd be doing things that didn't make sense, too. Like, I remember one night, I spent forty-five minutes rearranging the magazines in the dayroom by the color of the barcode on the back cover, instead of doing my rounds. I didn't even realize I was doing it until Brenda came in and yelled at me. 

So yeah, the words getting messed up, the disorganized stuff I do, and this whole... this whole thing with feeling like I'm constantly being monitored or watched... all of that has been going on together for about a year and a month now. It all started right around the same time.

Yeah, it's definitely still happening. It's actually... I think it's gotten a lot more specific lately. At first, like I was saying before, it was just this general feeling in the hallway or at my apartment, just this heavy feeling of eyes on me. But now? Now I know exactly who is doing it and how they're doing it. 

It's the supervisors. The nursing supervisors for the night shift. I mean, they've been completely messing with my schedule lately, constantly changing my shifts around. Usually, I'm on a pretty set rotation, right? Like, I know exactly what days I'm on the C-wing, what days I'm doing rounds. But suddenly, they're moving me to the admissions unit, then pulling me back to do quiet room observation, just constantly shifting my hours and my locations. And when I ask about it, or when I try to point it out to the other aides, they all just brush me off. They always tell me it's just staffing shortages. They're like, "Oh, you know two people quit last month, we just have to cover the gaps." 

But I know that's not true. I'm sure of it. I'm absolutely sure the supervisors changed my shifts specifically so they can watch me. And they're doing it through the unit cameras. We have these little black dome cameras in the corners of the ceilings—supposedly they're just for patient safety, to make sure nobody is getting into fights in the dayroom or whatever. But I know they're using them to monitor me. I can literally feel the lenses tracking me when I walk down the hall with the linen carts. I'll stop, and I can almost hear the little motors inside the cameras whirring to focus in on my face. 

They're doing it to see if I'm unsafe. That's the word they use, I just know it. Because of the things I've been doing, like with the magazines or when my words get all mixed up when I talk to Brenda... they think I'm a risk now. They think I'm an unsafe worker. So they sit up in the security office or the supervisor's lounge, just staring at the monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just trying to wipe down the tables or check the supply closet. They want to catch me doing something wrong so they can prove I'm unsafe and get rid of me. 

And it's just... it's so exhausting, you know? Trying to do your job when you know there's a camera lens following your every single move. I try to tell the other guys on my shift, I try to say, "Look at the camera, it just tracked me," but they just repeat that same line about staffing shortages, like they've been programmed to say it. But I know the truth. I know they're watching me.

I've always been really careful about it. And especially not right now, with how my head is already feeling so scrambled and my words are getting all tied up like I was just saying. I can't even imagine adding alcohol or drugs into this mess. It would just make everything a thousand times worse, wouldn't it? So, no, absolutely nothing like that. Not even a beer on the weekends. I just drink coffee, honestly. Lots and lots of coffee from the breakroom vending machine to stay awake for the overnight shifts, which probably tastes like dirt, but it keeps me upright. But yeah, definitely no drugs or alcohol.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing or seeing things that aren't there?\n\nPatient: No, no, I haven't. Um, I know that's a thing that happens to a lot of the patients I work with, you know? They'll be staring at a blank wall having a full-blown argument with someone who isn't there, or swatting at things in the air that don't exist, but for me? No. I don't get any of that. \n\nI mean, don't get me wrong, working the overnight shift, your eyes can play tricks on you when you're staring down a long, dim hallway at three in the morning. Sometimes the fluorescent lights flicker in the C-wing—maintenance never fixes them because we're just the night shift, right, so we're always the bottom priority—and you might think you see a shadow move out of the corner of your eye. But if I turn and look, it's always just a linen cart, or a mop bucket someone left out, or maybe a patient who got up to pace around. I always know what it actually is. \n\nAnd hearing things... honestly, the ward is noisy enough as it is without my brain making things up. The ice machine down the hall makes this huge clunking sound every forty-five minutes that sounds exactly like someone dropping a heavy work boot on the linoleum, and the HVAC system has this constant, low hum that vibrates right through the soles of your shoes. So I hear all of that. But it's all real stuff, you know? I'm not hearing voices in my head or seeing visions or anything like that. I know exactly what's actually in the room with me. It's really just the talking thing I told you about, how my own words get all smashed together and I can't keep my sentences straight. But I'm definitely not seeing or hearing anything that isn't really there.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your thoughts are racing or speeding by really fast when this happens?\n\nPatient: No, not really. It's not like that. It's not a speed thing, you know? Like, when I see the patients who are really manic, the ones who come in and they haven't slept in five days and they're pacing the dayroom at two in the morning, you can tell their brains are just going a million miles an hour. They talk so fast you can barely catch every third word, and they act like there's a motor inside them that just won't shut off. But that's not what's happening to me at all. \n\nMy thoughts aren't racing. They're just... getting lost on the way out, I guess? Like, the speed is totally normal. If I'm thinking about the patient charts, I'm just thinking about them at a regular, boring, everyday pace. But then when I open my mouth to talk about the charts, the words just sort of... take a detour. It's like I'm driving the speed limit, completely normal, but someone swapped all the road signs on me, so I end up in a totally different town without even realizing I took a wrong turn. \n\nI'm not feeling rushed or pressured or anything. I was actually trying to be really careful and clear because I knew the day nurse, Brenda, was already annoyed that I was running a few minutes late with the handover. I was speaking at a totally normal pace. It just didn't make any sense. So, no, it's definitely not that my thoughts are racing or speeding by. It's just the words themselves that are all wrong.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling unusually sad, anxious, or irritable lately?\n\nPatient: Yeah, sad. Definitely sad. I mean, not just sad like, \"Oh, I had a bad day at work,\" but this deep, heavy kind of sad that just... it doesn't go away. It's like I wake up in the afternoon, because of the night shift, right? Like there's nothing inside me but lead. \n\nAnd it's most days now. It really is. I try to tell myself, you know, \"You have a job, you're paying rent, you're doing fine,\" but my brain just doesn't care. It just feels like everything is pointless and exhausting. Little things at first. Like, I'd be walking down the C-wing, and I'd get this intense, prickling sensation on the back of my neck, like someone's eyes were just boring into me. I thought maybe it was one of the patients, you know, staring out from their room, but I'd turn around and the hallway would be completely empty. And then it started happening in the breakroom, too. I'd be sitting there, trying to eat my lukewarm microwave dinner at 2 AM, and I'd just know, with absolute certainty, that someone—or something—was observing me. Monitoring me. \n\nAnd it wasn't just at the hospital, either. I'd go home to my apartment, lock the door, pull the blinds down tight, and I still couldn't shake the feeling. I'd sit on my couch in the dark, just waiting, listening to the pipes creak, completely convinced that there were cameras hidden in the vents or that the neighbors were tracking my movements through the floorboards. They want to catch me doing something wrong so they can prove I'm unsafe and get rid of me. \n\nAnd it's just... it's so exhausting, you know? Trying to do your job when you know there's a camera lens following your every single move. They sit up there in the security room or the lounge with their little monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just tying up a laundry bag or wiping down a mattress, just waiting for me to do something weird or mess up my words again so they can finally prove I'm an unsafe worker and get rid of me. \n\nAnd it just... it drives me insane because nobody else gets it. Even when people tell me it’s just staffing shortages, I know that's a total lie. They're just covering for the supervisors, or they're too blind to see it. You don't just bounce one guy around every single unit in the building unless you're trying to keep him right under those black dome cameras at all times. So yeah, I know they're doing it. Well, maybe not right this second because I'm sitting here with you, but the second I badge back into that hospital tonight, I know those lenses are going to lock right back onto me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the supervisors' alleged monitoring of you is a plot to harm you or is it just to assess your job performance?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't think they are going to, like, jump out of a supply closet and physically attack me or anything like that. I'll stop, and I can almost hear the little motors inside the cameras whirring to focus in on my face. \n\nThey're doing it to see if I'm unsafe. That's the word they use, I just know it. Because of the things I've been doing, like with the magazines or when my words get all mixed up when I talk to Brenda... they think I'm a risk now. They think I'm an unsafe worker. So they sit up in the security office or the supervisor's lounge, just staring at the monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just trying to wipe down the tables or check the supply closet. They want to catch me doing something wrong so they can prove I'm unsafe and get rid of me. \n\nAnd it's just... it's so exhausting, you know? Trying to do your job when you know there's a camera lens following your every single move. I try to tell the other guys on my shift, I try to say, \"Look at the camera, it just tracked me,\" but they just repeat that same line about staffing shortages, like they've been programmed to say it. They sit up there in the security room or the lounge with their little monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just tying up a laundry bag or wiping down a mattress, just waiting for me to do something weird or mess up my words again so they can finally prove I'm an unsafe worker and get rid of me. \n\nAnd it just... it drives me insane because nobody else gets it. A misunderstanding? Doc, come on. I work there. I know what the standard security measures are. I've been an aide there for long enough to know how things actually run. I know that the general cameras in the hallways are supposed to be for, like, if a patient elopes, or if there's a code gray and security needs to see where a fight broke out. They are watching me to see if I'm unsafe, and they're hiding it behind this whole fake scheduling crisis, and honestly, I just don't get why you can't see that. Well, yeah, it all started the exact day they messed with my schedule. I mean, I feel like I keep saying the same thing, but you have to understand how this actually went down to get why I'm so sure about it.

And suddenly I just get this... this really intense feeling. Like the hair on the back of my neck literally stood up.

I know how our security system works—a blinking red light means someone in the supervisor's office has manually overridden the auto-pan and is actively controlling the camera with the joystick. 

That was the moment. That was when all the puzzle pieces just snapped together in my head. 

The sudden shift change, pulling me off my regular floor, Dave feeding me that garbage about staffing shortages... it was all a setup. I realized right then and there that I am absolutely sure the supervisors changed my shifts just so they could put me on that specific ward and watch me through the unit cameras. They were sitting in that office, zoomed in on my hands, just waiting for me to make one tiny mistake so they could write me up and terminate me. 

And ever since that Thursday, it hasn't stopped. Every single time I work, I see the cameras track me. So yeah, that was the specific incident, but it's not just an incident anymore, doc. It's my entire life at that hospital now.

Well, I mean, the schedule change was the big one, the main stress.
